```{r} 
data_path <- Sys.getenv("STATCAST_DATA_PATH")

hitters <- read.csv(file.path(data_path, "FullStatcastData.csv"))
```

# Introduction to Simple fWAR Models

The first stage of the modeling process focuses on developing simple linear regression models to predict player value as measured by FanGraphs Wins Above Replacement (fWAR). Rather than immediately building complex models with multiple predictors, this section examines the relationship between fWAR and one explanatory variable at a time. Looking at each variable separately provides a clear starting point for understanding which statistics are most closely related to overall player value before accounting for the effects of other variables.

Simple linear regression also provides an important baseline for the rest of the project. By modeling each predictor separately, it is possible to compare how well traditional offensive statistics, advanced sabermetric metrics, and Statcast measurements explain differences in fWAR. This allows the analysis to directly compare older, more familiar statistics with newer measures designed to capture player performance and underlying skill more effectively.

The models in this section will focus on several different categories of baseball statistics. Traditional measures such as home runs, batting average, and RBI will be compared with advanced metrics such as wOBA, wRC+, and Off. Statcast measures, including xwOBA, Barrel%, HardHit%, and average exit velocity, will also be examined. Because these statistics measure different aspects of performance, comparing them individually can help determine which types of metrics have the strongest relationships with overall player value.

Simple regression models are also useful because their results are relatively easy to interpret. Each model estimates the expected change in fWAR associated with a one-unit increase in the predictor. Model fit will be evaluated using measures such as R² and adjusted R², while residual error and statistical significance will provide additional information about the strength and reliability of each relationship. These results will later be compared with the more comprehensive models developed throughout the project.

An important goal of this section is not to assume that a single statistic can fully explain player value. fWAR incorporates offensive, defensive, and baserunning contributions, so a statistic that focuses on only one part of a player's performance may have limited explanatory power on its own. Instead, these simple models are intended to identify useful predictors and establish a baseline against which more advanced models can be evaluated.

The results from this section will provide the foundation for the multiple regression analysis developed later in the project. Variables that show strong relationships with fWAR can be considered as candidates for more comprehensive models, while variables with weaker relationships or substantial overlap with other predictors can be examined further using multicollinearity diagnostics and model-selection techniques. Ultimately, this section establishes the first comparison between traditional statistics, advanced sabermetrics, and Statcast measures and helps determine how much additional information modern baseball metrics provide when evaluating player value.


## Traditional Statistics Models

The first group of simple linear regression models examined traditional offensive statistics and their individual relationships with fWAR. The variables included batting average (BA), home runs (HR), runs batted in (RBI), runs scored (R), stolen bases (SB), on-base plus slugging (OPS), walk percentage (BB%), and strikeout percentage (K%). These statistics represent some of the most commonly used measures of offensive performance and provide a useful baseline for comparing traditional baseball evaluation methods with the advanced sabermetric and Statcast measures examined later.

The results show that traditional statistics vary considerably in how well they explain differences in fWAR. OPS produced the strongest individual traditional model, with an R² of 0.572 and an adjusted R² of 0.572. This indicates that approximately 57.2% of the variation in fWAR was explained by OPS alone. Runs scored was the second strongest traditional measure, with an R² of 0.524 and an adjusted R² of 0.524. Batting average explained approximately 33.2% of the variation in fWAR, while home runs and RBI explained approximately 23.1% and 22.2%, respectively.

The remaining traditional statistics showed substantially weaker relationships with fWAR. BB% explained approximately 12.8% of the variation, while stolen bases explained approximately 9.6%. Strikeout percentage produced the weakest model, with an R² of only 0.0115 and an adjusted R² of 0.0108. Although K% was statistically significant, it explained only about 1.2% of the variation in fWAR. This demonstrates an important distinction between statistical significance and explanatory power. With a relatively large sample, a variable can have a statistically significant relationship with fWAR while still providing limited information about differences in overall player value.

All eight traditional predictors were statistically significant in their respective simple regression models. The estimated relationships were generally consistent with their expected direction. BA, HR, RBI, R, SB, OPS, and BB% all had positive coefficients, meaning higher values were associated with higher fWAR. K% had a negative coefficient, indicating that higher strikeout rates were associated with lower fWAR. However, the strength of these relationships varied substantially, as shown by the differences in R² values across the models.

The estimated coefficients also provide an interpretable measure of the relationship between each statistic and fWAR. For example, the OPS model had an estimated coefficient of approximately 17.15, meaning that a one-unit increase in OPS was associated with an estimated 17.15-unit increase in fWAR within the fitted model. Similarly, the estimated coefficient for runs scored was approximately 0.0817, indicating that each additional run was associated with an estimated increase of approximately 0.082 fWAR. These coefficients should be interpreted within the scale and range of each statistic rather than directly compared across variables with different measurement units.

The diagnostic plots generally indicated that the simple regression models were reasonable for use as baseline models, although some patterns were observed. The HR, OPS, and BB% models showed some evidence of increasing residual variability in their Scale-Location plots, suggesting possible mild heteroskedasticity. The Residuals vs. Leverage plots also showed a generally increasing pattern as fitted values increased. These patterns were not considered severe enough to prevent the models from being used as baseline comparisons, but they provide justification for examining model assumptions and potential heteroskedasticity more carefully in the later diagnostic sections of the project.

Overall, the results demonstrate that traditional statistics can provide meaningful information about player value, but their explanatory power differs substantially across metrics. OPS and runs scored were the strongest traditional measures, while BA provided a moderate relationship with fWAR. HR and RBI also showed meaningful relationships, but explained considerably less variation than OPS and runs scored. In contrast, SB, BB%, and especially K% provided relatively limited explanatory power when considered individually.

These results establish an important baseline for the remainder of the analysis. Traditional statistics clearly contain useful information about player value, but the differences between individual metrics suggest that statistics capturing broader aspects of offensive performance may provide a more complete picture of player value. The next section examines advanced sabermetric measures to determine whether metrics specifically designed to evaluate overall player contribution can explain more variation in fWAR than traditional statistics.

```{r}
###############################################################
# Traditional Statistics Models
###############################################################
# Simple Linear Regression Models
# Each traditional statistic is modeled individually against
# fWAR to evaluate its relationship with overall player value.

model_BA <- lm(WAR ~ BA, data = hitters)

model_HR <- lm(WAR ~ HR, data = hitters)

model_RBI <- lm(WAR ~ RBI, data = hitters)

model_R <- lm(WAR ~ R, data = hitters)

model_SB <- lm(WAR ~ SB, data = hitters)

model_OPS <- lm(WAR ~ OPS, data = hitters)

model_BB <- lm(WAR ~ BB_Percent, data = hitters)

model_K <- lm(WAR ~ K_Percent, data = hitters)


# Regression Summaries

summary(model_BA)

summary(model_HR)

summary(model_RBI)

summary(model_R)

summary(model_SB)

summary(model_OPS)

summary(model_BB)

summary(model_K)


# 95% Confidence Intervals

confint(model_BA)

confint(model_HR)

confint(model_RBI)

confint(model_R)

confint(model_SB)

confint(model_OPS)

confint(model_BB)

confint(model_K)


# Traditional Statistics Model Comparison


traditional_models <- list(
  BA = model_BA,
  HR = model_HR,
  RBI = model_RBI,
  R = model_R,
  SB = model_SB,
  OPS = model_OPS,
  BB_Percent = model_BB,
  K_Percent = model_K
)

traditional_results <- data.frame(
  R2 = sapply(
    traditional_models,
    function(x) summary(x)$r.squared
  ),

  Adjusted_R2 = sapply(
    traditional_models,
    function(x) summary(x)$adj.r.squared
  ),

  Coefficient = sapply(
    traditional_models,
    function(x) coef(x)[2]
  ),

  P_Value = sapply(
    traditional_models,
    function(x) summary(x)$coefficients[2, 4]
  )
)

traditional_results


# Diagnostic Plots


par(mfrow = c(2,2))
plot(model_BA)
par(mfrow = c(1,1))


par(mfrow = c(2,2))
plot(model_HR)
par(mfrow = c(1,1))


par(mfrow = c(2,2))
plot(model_RBI)
par(mfrow = c(1,1))


par(mfrow = c(2,2))
plot(model_R)
par(mfrow = c(1,1))


par(mfrow = c(2,2))
plot(model_SB)
par(mfrow = c(1,1))


par(mfrow = c(2,2))
plot(model_OPS)
par(mfrow = c(1,1))


par(mfrow = c(2,2))
plot(model_BB)
par(mfrow = c(1,1))


par(mfrow = c(2,2))
plot(model_K)
par(mfrow = c(1,1))
```

## Advanced Sabermetric Models

The second group of simple linear regression models examined advanced sabermetric measures and their relationships with fWAR. These models included weighted On-Base Average (wOBA), Weighted Runs Created Plus (wRC+), Isolated Power (ISO), Offensive Runs (Off), Baserunning Runs (BsR), and Defensive Runs (Def). Unlike traditional statistics that focus primarily on individual outcomes such as hits, home runs, or runs batted in, these metrics are designed to provide a broader measurement of a player's offensive, baserunning, and defensive contributions. Each metric was modeled separately to determine how much variation in fWAR could be explained by each measure on its own.

The advanced sabermetric models generally explained substantially more variation in fWAR than the traditional statistics examined in Section 4.2. Offensive Runs (Off) produced the strongest individual model, with an R² of 0.736 and an adjusted R² of 0.736. This means that approximately 73.6% of the variation in fWAR was explained by Off in the simple regression model. Weighted Runs Created Plus (wRC+) was the second strongest model, explaining approximately 63.1% of the variation in fWAR. wOBA also demonstrated a strong relationship with fWAR, with an R² of approximately 0.600.

The remaining sabermetric metrics showed weaker but still statistically significant relationships with fWAR. ISO explained approximately 27.2% of the variation in fWAR, while Defensive Runs (Def) and Baserunning Runs (BsR) explained approximately 15.1% and 11.0%, respectively. These differences demonstrate that not all advanced metrics provide the same amount of information about overall player value. Offensive value measures such as Off, wRC+, and wOBA showed considerably stronger individual relationships with fWAR than the isolated baserunning and defensive measures.

All six sabermetric variables were statistically significant in their individual models, with p-values below 0.001. However, as with the traditional statistics, statistical significance alone does not indicate that a metric is a strong explanatory variable. The R² values provide a better indication of how much variation in fWAR is captured by each model. For example, BsR was statistically significant but explained only about 11.0% of the variation in fWAR, while Off explained approximately 73.6%. This difference highlights the importance of considering both statistical significance and explanatory power when comparing player evaluation metrics.

The estimated coefficients were also consistent with the expected direction of the relationships. Higher values of wOBA, wRC+, ISO, Off, BsR, and Def were associated with higher fWAR. The confidence intervals for each predictor excluded zero, providing additional evidence that these relationships were statistically significant within the simple regression framework. The relatively narrow confidence intervals for the coefficients also reflect the strong statistical evidence provided by the large sample.

Diagnostic analysis indicated that most of the sabermetric models did not show major issues that would immediately invalidate the simple regression approach. Some patterns were observed in the wOBA, wRC+, and ISO models. In particular, the Scale-Location plots showed a generally increasing pattern, suggesting that the variability of the residuals may increase somewhat as fitted values increase. The Residuals vs. Leverage plots also showed increasing leverage patterns at higher fitted values. These patterns were not considered severe enough to prevent the models from being used as baseline comparisons, but they indicate that variance and influential observations should be examined further in the project's later diagnostic analysis.

Overall, the results show that advanced sabermetric metrics provide considerably stronger individual relationships with fWAR than many traditional statistics. Off produced the strongest simple model, followed by wRC+ and wOBA, while ISO, Def, and BsR provided more limited explanatory power. These results provide evidence that metrics designed to measure broader aspects of player contribution can capture more of the variation in overall player value than many traditional statistics. The findings also provide a useful baseline for the Statcast models in the next section, where measures of underlying offensive skill will be evaluated against both traditional and sabermetric approaches.

```{r}
###############################################################
# Advanced Sabermetric Models
###############################################################

# Simple Linear Regression Models


model_woba <- lm(WAR ~ wOBA, data = hitters)

model_wrc <- lm(WAR ~ wRC_plus, data = hitters)

model_iso <- lm(WAR ~ ISO, data = hitters)

model_off <- lm(WAR ~ Off, data = hitters)

model_bsr <- lm(WAR ~ BsR, data = hitters)

model_def <- lm(WAR ~ Def, data = hitters)


# Regression Summaries


summary(model_woba)

summary(model_wrc)

summary(model_iso)

summary(model_off)

summary(model_bsr)

summary(model_def)


# 95% Confidence Intervals


confint(model_woba)

confint(model_wrc)

confint(model_iso)

confint(model_off)

confint(model_bsr)

confint(model_def)


# Advanced Sabermetric Model Comparison


advanced_models <- list(
  wOBA = model_woba,
  wRC_plus = model_wrc,
  ISO = model_iso,
  Off = model_off,
  BsR = model_bsr,
  Def = model_def
)

advanced_model_results <- data.frame(
  R2 = sapply(
    advanced_models,
    function(x) summary(x)$r.squared
  ),
  
  Adjusted_R2 = sapply(
    advanced_models,
    function(x) summary(x)$adj.r.squared
  ),
  
  Coefficient = sapply(
    advanced_models,
    function(x) coef(x)[2]
  ),
  
  P_Value = sapply(
    advanced_models,
    function(x) summary(x)$coefficients[2, 4]
  )
)

advanced_model_results


# Diagnostic Plots


par(mfrow = c(2,2))
plot(model_woba)
par(mfrow = c(1,1))


par(mfrow = c(2,2))
plot(model_wrc)
par(mfrow = c(1,1))


par(mfrow = c(2,2))
plot(model_iso)
par(mfrow = c(1,1))


par(mfrow = c(2,2))
plot(model_off)
par(mfrow = c(1,1))


par(mfrow = c(2,2))
plot(model_bsr)
par(mfrow = c(1,1))


par(mfrow = c(2,2))
plot(model_def)
par(mfrow = c(1,1))
```

## Statcast Models

The Statcast models examine whether newer measurements of player performance and underlying skill are associated with overall player value as measured by fWAR. These models include expected statistics such as xwOBA, xBA, xSLG, and xISO, along with measurements of contact quality such as Barrel%, Hard-Hit%, average exit velocity, launch angle, and Sweet Spot%. Unlike traditional statistics, which describe what happened on the field, several of these metrics are designed to estimate the quality of contact and expected outcomes behind those results.

All nine Statcast models produced statistically significant relationships with fWAR. However, statistical significance alone does not indicate that a variable is a strong predictor of player value. The amount of variation explained by each model was more important when comparing the usefulness of the different Statcast metrics.

Among the models, xwOBA produced the strongest relationship with fWAR, with an R² of 0.351 and an adjusted R² of 0.350. The estimated coefficient for xwOBA was 34.50, with a 95% confidence interval from approximately 32.01 to 36.98. This indicates a strong positive relationship between expected offensive production and overall player value. xSLG was the next strongest expected statistic, with an R² of 0.265, followed by xBA with an R² of 0.210. xISO explained approximately 17.6% of the variation in fWAR, making it weaker than the other expected offensive measures examined.

The direct Statcast contact-quality measurements generally explained less variation in fWAR. Barrel% had an R² of 0.113, while average exit velocity had an R² of 0.104 and Hard-Hit% had an R² of 0.084. Although all three variables had statistically significant positive relationships with fWAR, their lower R² values suggest that contact quality by itself does not explain as much of a player's overall value as broader measures of offensive production. This is reasonable because fWAR incorporates more than just the quality of contact, including offensive, defensive, and baserunning contributions.

Launch angle and Sweet Spot% showed the weakest relationships among the Statcast variables. Launch angle had an R² of only 0.020, while Sweet Spot% had an R² of 0.045. Both relationships were statistically significant, but the relatively small R² values indicate that these variables alone explain very little of the variation in fWAR. This demonstrates why statistical significance should not be interpreted as evidence that a variable is highly useful for prediction.

The diagnostic plots also provided an initial assessment of the regression assumptions. The first seven models showed gradual increases in the Scale-Location and Residuals vs. Leverage plots, while the Launch Angle model showed a gradual decrease. The Sweet Spot% model did not show a notable pattern in these plots. These patterns were relatively minor and were not considered substantial enough at this stage to invalidate the models. More detailed diagnostic testing and potential adjustments will be addressed in the later modeling sections.

Overall, the results show that Statcast and expected metrics provide meaningful information about player value, but their performance varies considerably by metric. xwOBA was the strongest individual Statcast-related predictor in this analysis, while launch angle and Sweet Spot% provided relatively little explanatory power on their own. Importantly, these results also suggest that newer Statcast measurements do not automatically outperform traditional or advanced sabermetric statistics. The stronger expected metrics will therefore be considered as candidates for the multiple regression models in the next section, where their predictive value can be evaluated alongside other sources of player information.

```{r}

# Simple Linear Regression Models


model_xwoba <- lm(WAR ~ xwOBA, data = hitters)

model_xba <- lm(WAR ~ xBA, data = hitters)

model_xslg <- lm(WAR ~ xSLG, data = hitters)

model_xiso <- lm(WAR ~ xISO, data = hitters)

model_barrel <- lm(WAR ~ Barrel_Percent, data = hitters)

model_hardhit <- lm(WAR ~ HardHit_Percent, data = hitters)

model_la <- lm(WAR ~ LaunchAngle_Avg, data = hitters)

model_sweetspot <- lm(WAR ~ SweetSpot_Percent, data = hitters)


# Regression Summaries


summary(model_xwoba)

summary(model_xba)

summary(model_xslg)

summary(model_xiso)

summary(model_barrel)

summary(model_hardhit)

summary(model_ev)

summary(model_la)

summary(model_sweetspot)



# 95% Confidence Intervals


confint(model_xwoba)

confint(model_xba)

confint(model_xslg)

confint(model_xiso)

confint(model_barrel)

confint(model_hardhit)

confint(model_ev)

confint(model_la)

confint(model_sweetspot)


# Statcast Model Comparison


statcast_models <- list(
  xwOBA = model_xwoba,
```
